headline: Shipping is one of four halls at Gastech, and the constraint nobody controls
deck: Liquefaction capacity can be built to a schedule. The carriers to move it are ordered years earlier from a handful of yards.
excerpt: Gastech's floor is organised into four areas, one of them Shipping and Marine. With Gulf liquefaction capacity arriving late this decade, the vessels to carry it are being ordered now from a shipbuilding sector with limited slots.
content:
The Gastech exhibition floor is organised into four dedicated areas, and Shipping and Marine is the one where the physical constraint on the LNG trade actually sits.

Liquefaction gets the attention because it is where the capital concentrates. A train is a multi-billion dollar process plant with a visible construction programme. But a liquefaction plant without carriers is a plant that cannot deliver, and the carrier fleet is built by a small number of shipyards, principally in South Korea and China, with order books that fill years in advance.

The arithmetic is straightforward and unforgiving. A single LNG carrier is a specialised vessel with cryogenic containment, and it costs a substantial fraction of what a small liquefaction train costs. The number of vessels a trade route needs depends on the distance: a cargo moving from the Gulf to Japan ties up a ship for far longer per delivery than one moving from the Gulf to India, so the same tonnage of exports requires a different fleet depending on where it goes.

That is why the destination question matters beyond price. Qatar's expansion from 77 to 142 million tonnes a year, the Emirates' 9.6 million tonnes at Ruwais, and the United States tranche arriving in the same period together imply a large addition to the world fleet, ordered against assumptions about who buys and from how far away.

Marine fuel is the second thread in the same hall, and it runs the other way. LNG as a bunker fuel has moved from demonstration to a real segment, driven by tightening emissions regulation on shipping. That creates demand for bunkering infrastructure at major ports — storage, transfer systems, bunker vessels — which is a terminal engineering business rather than a shipping one, and one where Gulf ports have an obvious geographic case given their position on the Asia-Europe route.

The engineering content of both is substantial and specific. Cryogenic transfer at scale involves materials selection at minus 162 degrees, boil-off management, custody transfer metering accurate enough to settle cargoes worth tens of millions of dollars, and safety systems designed around a release scenario that behaves unlike any hydrocarbon liquid.

For the Gulf's industrial base the opportunity is in terminals rather than hulls. Shipbuilding at this specification is not moving to the region, but bunkering infrastructure, terminal equipment, maintenance and the marine services around them are all within reach of yards that already serve the offshore sector.

Gastech runs at BITEC Bangkok from 14 to 17 September, with more than 1,000 exhibitors expected.
